samples.text: It is good that there are some drugs like ketamine and 5-MeO-DMT which can help people with super fortified egos to go beyond their ego. Unfortunately, what usually ends up happening with such super dissociating drugs is something called "Spritual Bypassing," in which people avoid doing the inner child reparenting therapy to heal their traumas, and instead they use a drug like this, or even spirituality in general, to completely dissociate and dis-identify with all their traumas.

As explained in my Ultimate Psychedelic post, I recently discovered that although I normally hate how 5-MeO-DMT feels, if I just sniff some raw apple vinegar right before I use 5-MeO-DMT, the experience is really so incredible lovely! It also helps a lot to consume ZHoly3O so that the parasite die-off toxins are mopped up before they damage the experience and your health. I would also recommend smelling Metta NMT humic acid and eating coffee cherry, as explained in my Haoma guide.

Okay, write it. Write the unfair version too if that's what is there. The only rule is that it stays private for now. Later you can look at it and go, ugh, no, that's just mean. And then maybe two lines down there's the actual no you were trying to say. Keep that. If you owe an apology, put that in too. Sometimes the whole useful response turns out to be three boring lines. Sometimes, after all that typing, you don't really have anything to send.

Write the furious version somewhere private. I'm serious: if twelve sentences are already screaming to get out, pretending you have only two civilized ones probably won't make you wiser. Just don't send it yet. Come back when you've cooled off a little and see what's still true. Maybe you were unfair. Maybe you also finally said no. Keep the no. Add the apology if you owe one. The useful reply might be shorter, or there might not be one. If you say you'll answer tomorrow, mean tomorrow.

If closing your eyes starts making the room disappear, open them and look around. Of course, the point isn't that closed eyes are bad; it's whether you still know where you are, what time it is, and can feel your body here. You're not trying to prove anything by staying in it. If these sessions keep leaving you more disoriented, more compelled, or less able to function afterward, make them shorter and get some grounded support.

But here’s the chicken-and-egg problem. What if you’re so far inside the child-state that you can’t become the adult? This is much easier when you can already reach one of those adult roles. Without that, you can sit there trying to say all the loving things while the old critic, numbness, panic, or urge to get away is running the whole thing.

When people spiritually bypass their inner child traumas, they end up using spirituality as an excuse for their harmful behaviors. This is seen in pretty much every guru, with very rare exception. They say things like "We Are All One," or they claim to be God, and this means they can do whatever they want (which is the Free Masonic creed, "Do As Thou Wilt").

Unlike most other psychedelics, 5-MeO-DMT is extremely dangerous. Even taking 1/3 too much for you might be deadly, or permanently mind-shattering (according to a personal conversation I had with the admin of 5meodmt.org years ago). If combined with drugs that boost dopamine or serotonin (or MAOIs like in ayahuasca/harmalas/caapi/rue), the venom/5-MeO-DMT becomes much more deadly, but that doesn't stop certain people from promoting this risky combination. Make sure you investigate interactions between all the meds and supplements you take before using 5-MeO-DMT.

And then there is the person who wrote the ugly version. Don't throw them out with the draft. Read it once more after you've decided what to send and ask what they were trying so hard to get heard. Maybe they needed protection. Maybe reassurance, or actual help. Maybe they were furious and still had a point. An angry first draft can be terrible communication without being a childish protest. Cleaning up what you send is one job; staying on that person's side is another.

This is a question I always ask myself. Why do people choose to use 5-MeO-DMT, instead of ayahuasca (or especially the Ultimate Psychedelic), considering that 5-MeO-DMT has no tradition of human use, much less therapeutic value, and is known to be very dangerous compared to ayahuasca?

So far, I have come up with a few answers (comment if you have others!):

Super entrenched ego, due to psychopathy, narcissism, and/or (c)PTSD, which blocks their ability to get powerful transcendental experiences from ayahuasca or meditation. Or, because they wish to avoid the moralizing guiding spirit (teacher) of ayahuasca.

They heard about it from someone and it seemed like it worked for that person, so they tried it and liked it, basically nothing to compare it to.

It’s vastly overhyped by some folks as being the God Molecule.

It’s harder to obtain than ayahuasca ingredients, which makes it seem more interesting.

It doesn’t have MAOi contraindications like ayahuasca, although it has its own set of dangerous interactions.

Some people’s neurochemistry is uniquely suited to 5-methoxy substituted tryptamines. These people find 5-MeO-DMT to be pleasurable, not frightening and toxic. The people who find it helpful for muting their emotional pain are also most at risk of abusing it.

There's a question I keep coming back to with inner work: am I actually processing something, or am I checking whether I've processed it? The hurt can be completely real either way. But if you're back at the same wound for the hundredth time mostly to see whether you've finally grieved it correctly, the healing itself can become the hook.

But here’s the chicken-and-egg problem. What if you’re so far inside the child-state that you can’t become the adult? This is much easier when you can already reach one of those adult roles. But when you can't, it's like you sit there trying to be loving while your mind is becoming controlled again by the inherited critic voice, or you start going numb, throwing a fit, or panicking.

You may not know for certain whether the other person is or could be capable of a healthier response, and neither do they. If they promise to change, that's probably as useful as their prior promises were. Think about how long it has taken you to become more healthy. Could you have done that from one moment to the next based on a promise? Sometimes we can be a better support for someone when we maintain a realistic boundary, so that we can hold high expectations, and still feel prepared for their failure to meet them.

It doesn't mean you need to hide your upset, or apply for a permit to protest, but choose your battles and execute them wisely, so you don't end up regretting how you communicated later. As Lao Tsu might have said (if I could ever have read that whole boring Art of War book), a war with no casualties is the best possible war. When high IQ & EQ communication hits a writer's block, sometimes the best thing is to simply say, "I need some time to think about my response." And if the conflict really requires a response right now, then obviously just do your best rather than wait for the perfect timing.

I also personally know a guy named Dan Conner, a 5-MeO-DMT facilitator, and it took me years to figure out he is some kind of sociopath (he hides it better than Ball, and many of my “friends” still trust him). What we can learn from this is that this substance and the “full release” ego death it can provide is not able to turn an evil person into a good person, and it might even do the opposite in some cases, especially since it seems like something which is healing that actually may not be.

Physical trauma reactions can persist after the danger has passed, even when you know you're safe. With complex or developmental trauma, direct work on the deepest memory can be overwhelming, so a gradual approach may be enough: Buddhist nun Pema Chodron calls it a “feather touch,” and Peter Levine, the founder of Somatic Experiencing, calls gentle work around the edges “pendulation.” The same limit appears in inner-child therapy: you can know what the younger part needs yet enter the child-state so fully that too little adult perspective remains to provide it.

After one terrible conversation, I can see why you'd want to make a call about the person right then. Then sometimes they come back later and actually talk about what you were trying to say. They still disagree. Their boundary is still exactly the one you hated. But you're talking about the thing now. So what, exactly, did the first fight prove? Other times the subject changes but the ending feels strangely familiar. [Lindsay Gibson](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VlNpgFWOLPw) writes about that kind of repeated pattern in her work on emotional immaturity: you bring up something that hurt you and somehow your part of it is gone by the end.

Don't be afraid to ask your therapist/yourself "What is this practice supposed to help, and how would I know if it's helping?" This sovereign, gently curious stance should apply to everything in life. Feeling calmer or having deeper insights or explanations for the trauma response are some possible signs of initial progress, but if that's the endgame, it's just a cope. Real healing is ultimately measured by reduced need for the therapy, just like real growing up is not something you do forever. And if the therapy is actually working, it should improve your daily life, and especially the health of the inner child-inner adult relationship. Going at it harder isn't as useful as going at it with more wisdom and compassion. Take the parts that work, and innovate on the rest.

Then there is whoever wrote the mess. I wouldn't make them disappear just because you managed to write a nicer text. Read the first version again. What were they trying to stop? What did they need somebody to understand? Maybe the answer is protection. Maybe reassurance. Maybe they were just furious and also right about one part of the argument. You can decide the draft should never leave your phone and still take its author seriously. Otherwise you've edited the message and missed the person.

The first draft is often the part of me that got hurt grabbing the pencil first. I don't want the adult to snatch it away because what came out was angry or messy or not especially skillful. Usually there was something real underneath it that I was trying to get across: this hurt, I need you to understand what happened, I need you to stop doing that, I need some help here. The adult can sit beside the child, keep his hand on the pencil, and help him find a way to say it that the other person might actually hear. But that's a different job from taking care of the person who wrote the first version. Maybe he needs protection, maybe reassurance, maybe actual help. Making the message better doesn't mean deciding the protest itself was childish just because it came out badly.
